#Remotes

A remote is a machine that carries services for this host — a VPS, or the very machine serviceman runs on. It runs serviceman-agent, which dials this host and waits for orders. serviceman never dials out, so the machine needs no open port, no public address and no key of yours — a box behind NAT works.

serviceman itself starts nothing: every container and every program is the work of an agent. A docker or a shell service names the remote it runs on, and a config with no remote can serve folders of pages and give addresses to what already runs, and nothing more.

The address stays here. grafana.example.com still points at the serviceman host; the container runs on the remote, and every request rides back through the link the agent dialled. The visitor sees no difference.

#Add a remote

+ Add remote on the control page asks for a name, makes the token for you, and writes it to the config. The remote appears under Remotes at once — offline, with the two ways to put the agent on that machine, filled in with its name, this host's address and its token.

By hand it is the same thing, with a secret of your own:

openssl rand -hex 32

"remotes": [
    {"name": "vps1", "title": "Example VPS", "token": "0c0f…a91b"}
]

#Put the agent on the machine

Three ways to the same agent. It needs node and nothing else — no npm install, no build. On a machine with no node, the install line says so before anything else, before the password --root asks for, and prints the command that puts node, one file, in ~/bin; the same install line run again finds it there.

#One file

curl -fsSL https://serviceman.example.com/api/v1/agent.js -o serviceman-agent.js
node serviceman-agent.js --url https://serviceman.example.com --token 0c0f…a91b

The token is the whole introduction. serviceman looks up the remote that holds it, so the agent gives no name and cannot claim one it has no token for. One token, one machine: while an agent holds the link, a second one on the same token is refused rather than taking it over.

serviceman builds that file out of its own modules every time it is asked for, so it can never be out of date. To carry it over yourself instead, bin/agent-bundle writes the same file here.

Option What it is
--url Where serviceman answers, or a socket file. SERVICEMAN_URL.
--token The token of this machine. SERVICEMAN_TOKEN.
--dir The folder whose free space is reported. SERVICEMAN_DIR, default /.
--docker The docker command on that machine. SERVICEMAN_DOCKER.
--once Dial once and exit when the link drops, instead of dialling again.

#An image

docker build -f Dockerfile.agent -t serviceman-agent .

docker run -d --name serviceman-agent --restart always \
    --network host \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -v /:/host:ro -e SERVICEMAN_DIR=/host \
    -e SERVICEMAN_URL=https://serviceman.example.com \
    -e SERVICEMAN_TOKEN=0c0f…a91b \
    serviceman-agent

The image is the one file on node:24-alpine, with a docker client beside it. Three things it needs from the machine: the docker socket, so it can run the containers it is asked for; --network host, so it reaches those containers where docker publishes them, on the loopback; and / mounted read-only with SERVICEMAN_DIR=/host, so the free space it reports is the machine's and not the container's.

#From a copy of the repo

rsync -a --exclude node_modules --exclude .git ./ vps1:/opt/serviceman/
ssh vps1 /opt/serviceman/bin/serviceman-agent --url … --token …

#What the installer leaves on the machine

One folder, and everything about that machine's half is inside it — /opt/serviceman-agent as root, ~/serviceman-agent otherwise:

agent.js       the agent, one file, node and nothing else
servermon.js   the machine's load every second, written and kept running by the agent
env            where the host is, and the token. Mode 600.
status         what the agent is doing right now, rewritten every few seconds
logs/agent/    the agent's log, one file a day: logs/agent/20260823.txt
logs/servermon/  servermon's, a JSON line a second, one file a day: logs/servermon/20260823.jsonl
services/      everything the host asked this machine to install, a folder each
bin/install    puts it under systemd, or says how to run it. Safe to run again.
bin/restart    starts it again — what a line added to env needs to take
bin/uninstall  stops it and takes it out of systemd
README.md      the same, on the machine, for whoever finds it there

Not root, it is kept up by your own systemd, and the one install line does all it takes. Your systemd runs only while you are logged in unless lingering is on, so bin/install turns lingering on first, asking for the sudo password once when you may not do it alone. A shell opened with su or sudo has no XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so systemctl --user there finds no bus; the scripts look for it at /run/user/<uid> themselves. With no sudo either, it says what to run as root and writes no unit: loginctl enable-linger <you>, then bin/install again.

status is for the moment the host is the thing that cannot be reached:

serviceman-agent 1.0.0 built 2026-08-23T11:32:17.607Z
pid 203911, up 4h 12m
machine laptop
host http://serviceman:3001
link online as remote laptop, for 4h 11m
programs
  writer#1 pid 204338 /opt/serviceman-agent/services/apps/writer
refreshed 2026-08-23T15:46:03.118Z

Everything the agent makes stays under that folder. A program the host installs here lands in services/<name>.<suffix>, one folder per service, and a path that would leave services/ is refused. So the machine is left as it was found: bin/uninstall, rm -rf the folder, and nothing of serviceman is anywhere else.

#Newer agents find their way over

The agent says which build it is when it dials in, and this host knows the build it serves. When they differ, the machine is asked to fetch the current one — it runs its own bin/update, which is the same thing you would run there by hand.

That check runs when a machine dials in and once a minute after that, so a machine that has been connected for a week hears about a newer agent too. A machine is asked again at most every ten minutes: an update replaces the agent, so being asked twice for the same build means the machine cannot update itself, and asking harder will not help.

[remote_update_asked]     remote=laptop running=2026-08-20T09:11:02.318Z serving=2026-08-23T16:03:50.546Z
[remote_update_refused]   remote=laptop reason="… is not here — this agent was not installed by the installer"
[remote_update_not_taken] remote=laptop running=2026-08-20T09:11:02.318Z serving=2026-08-23T16:03:50.546Z asked=3

An agent that answers "started" and dials in again as the same build did not update, whatever it said: each ask after that is remote_update_not_taken, and the machine's page says so under Agent. An agent recent enough to know keeps what its bin/update printed in logs/update.log and answers the next ask with it, as remote_update_refused.

"agent_update": false in the config leaves every machine as it is, to be updated by hand.

#Keep it up

bin/install does it — the system's systemd when run as root, your own systemd otherwise, with lingering so it survives a logout. It is written by the installer with the paths already in it, and running it again is how you pick up an edited env or a replaced agent.js.

Where there is no systemd, it says what to run instead:

env $(cat /opt/serviceman-agent/env | xargs) /usr/bin/node /opt/serviceman-agent/agent.js

With the image, --restart always does the same thing.

#A kind of machine, not one machine

A machine carries tags — what it is, written by whoever runs serviceman:

"remotes": [
    {"name": "vps1", "token": "0c0f…a91b", "tags": ["gpu", "eu"]},
    {"name": "vps2", "token": "7a1b…33cd", "tags": ["eu"]}
]

and a service asks for a kind of machine instead of a name:

{"name": "grafana", "type": "docker", "remotes": ["#gpu"], "image": "grafana/grafana:latest"}

remotes is still a list in the order it prefers, so ["vps1", "#eu"] means that machine if it is up, otherwise anything in Europe.

A machine also says what it is. The agent takes --tag, and what it says holds for as long as its link does:

serviceman-agent --url … --token 0c0f…a91b --tag gpu

[remote_online] remote=vps1 from=203.0.113.9 agent=1.0.0 tags=["eu","gpu"] machine=…

So a machine's tags come from two places: the config, which is the host's word and stands whether the machine is up or not, and the machine itself, which is gone the moment it disconnects. A machine written into the config holds a token of its own and is trusted with what it says; a machine that added itself holds the fleet's join token, so it may only ever claim what join.tags_allowed lists — on every link, not only the first.

Because a machine can say what it is at any time, a tag nothing carries yet is not a config error. The boot says so instead, once per tag:

[serviceman_tag_nowhere] tag=gpu service=grafana

which is also what a typo looks like — with the service reading waiting for its machine until something answers.

#A machine that adds itself

The point of a tag is a machine you have not written down yet. One secret lets it join:

"join": {"token": "0c0f…a91b", "tags_allowed": ["gpu", "eu"], "name_prefix": "auto-"}

serviceman-agent --url https://serviceman.example.com --token <the join token> --tag gpu

serviceman writes it into the config with a secret of its own, gives it the tags it was allowed to claim, and it starts carrying every service that asks for #gpu — including services that were waiting for a machine that did not exist when they were written.

[remote_joined] remote=auto-box-17 machine=box-17 from=203.0.113.9 tags=["gpu"] refused=["secret"]

The line says what it claimed and what was dropped. A tag in the config is a fact; a tag from a machine is a claim — only tags_allowed is honoured, because a machine that names its own tags is choosing which of your work it receives.

The machine says which machine it is (--machine, the hostname by default), so the same box coming back takes its own entry instead of leaving a dead one behind. That identity is worth exactly as much as the join token: whoever holds it can add a machine to your fleet and claim the allowed tags. Treat it as the password of the fleet, keep it out of images and shell history, and leave join out of the config entirely when you do not need it — which is the default.

#Run a service there

{
    "name": "grafana",
    "type": "docker",
    "remote": "vps1",
    "publish": {"host": "grafana.example.com", "port": 3000},
    "image": "grafana/grafana:latest"
}

serviceman drives docker over the link — run, start, stop, inspect, port, logs — and proxies the answers back through it. Everything else about a service works the way it does here: the idle policy, the pool, the waiting page, and Shell, which opens a stream to the docker socket over there and runs the exec through it.

A shell service names a remote the same way, and the agent runs the program as its own child. Nothing is placed for you, and nothing moves on its own: a service runs where you write it.

#What the host knows about a remote

The agent says what the machine is when the link opens — hostname, cpu, memory, free disk, docker version, node version — and repeats the numbers that move every 5 seconds: among them how busy its cores were, which is cpu use as top counts it, beside the load average, which counts what waits on disk and network too and so is no share of the cores. They are servermon's last line (below), read from its file: the agent measures nothing itself. While servermon is off or silent (its last line older than 5 seconds) the numbers are none, and the Overview and Health say so. This host pings the agent every 30 seconds for the delay, and sends a megabyte there and back every ten minutes for the speed. All of it is on the control page, and in /api/v1/status.

The Overview tab shows a machine at a glance: its state beside its name, its uptime in one row under it, then tiles for CPU, memory, disk and temperature, each with a bar under it (amber from 80%, red from 92%), and for its battery and the link; its history, then cards for the machine, its agent, its services, its updates and its logs, each with a link to the tab that does more with it, and its raw state folded away at the end. It is src/main/public/remote_overview.js.

History is the machine's charts: CPU, memory, the space on all its disks together (as the remotes list counts it; the Disk tile is the one / is on), disk I/O, network, open tcp connections and ping, over the last hour, day, week or month. The agent keeps the numbers on its own disk, under metrics/ in its folder, whether serviceman is there or not: a line every 30 seconds made from servermon's lines of that half minute, for two days, and five-minute averages for 90 days, a few megabytes at most. Ping is the time from each of its beats to serviceman's answer. The page reads a range when it opens and every half minute after, from GET /api/v1/remotes/<name>/metrics?range=1h|24h|7d|30d, which asks the agent and keeps nothing but the last answer for each range: that answer is shown while the machine is offline, marked with the time it was read. The minutes a machine was off are a gap in its lines. The cursor runs through every chart at once, so a spike in one is read against the others. An agent before 1.9 has no charts, and the pane says how to update it.

Uptime is a bar a day for the last 30, in one row under the machine's name, its share of those days at the end of it: green when servermon wrote a line every second of it, orange from 99%, red below, grey for the days before servermon came. A gap of more than 10 seconds between two lines is a stretch the machine was down; a day pointed at or tapped says, in a box under it, its share and its longest stretches, in the machine's own time zone, each with why: rebooted (the line after it says another boot time), servermon stopped or the machine slept (the same one), or no line since. The agent counts the lines itself and reads each byte of them once: a finished day when it first meets it (the time and boot at the start of each line, about 170 ms for a day's 50 MB), today from where the last count stopped, every minute. The count is kept in metrics/uptime.json, 90 days, longer than servermon keeps its files. The page reads it from GET /api/v1/remotes/<name>/uptime?days=30 when it opens and every minute after, and shows the last answer while the machine is offline; the Remotes list has the last 30 days as a share on each card, and as the same row of bars, a day each, when a machine's row is opened in its table. An agent before 1.22 has none, and the pane says how to update it.

servermon is the one thing that reads the machine, second by second, and the night it stopped answering is in it too: CPU and steal, load, memory and swap, how long tasks waited for the CPU, memory and disk, every disk's space (a ZFS pool counted once: its folders' used space and the pool's free room), busy time and bytes read and written, network in, out, drops and errors, open and half-open tcp connections, connections refused at a full queue, the conntrack table, temperature, battery, and pings to the gateway and to two internet hosts, each line starting with its time and the machine's boot time. One JSON line a second into logs/servermon/<yyyymmdd>.jsonl beside the agent, 30 days kept, read on the machine with tail and jq. It is src/servermon/servermon.js, one file with node and nothing else; the agent writes it into its folder and starts it on its own, so a restart or an update of the agent leaves it running, and finds it again by its command line. The agent looks every minute: one that is gone, an older text, or one silent for half a minute is started again (servermon_begin). bin/uninstall stops it. It runs wherever the agent keeps a log folder: the install line, bin/serviceman-agent and the agent's docker image all give it one. An agent with SERVICEMAN_LOG_DIR unset or none has no servermon and so no numbers; bin/status, the Overview and Health say so.

One more thing its page reads on the spot and keeps nowhere. Processes is every process on that machine, as the tree it is: each one under the one that started it, and a branch folds away. Typing in its box keeps the processes whose command, user or pid match, with the ones above them dimmed so each keeps its place in the tree; List lists them heaviest CPU first instead, and a column's header sorts by it, RSS for the heaviest in memory. It is ps run over there when the pane opens and when Read again is pressed, never on a clock. The ports it listens on are in the Firewall tab, below.

Disks is every filesystem mounted there, from df, and What takes the space counts where a disk's space went: its folders, biggest first, each with its share, and a click on one opens the folders inside it. It is du -x run over there, on that disk alone, when asked: a minute on a big disk. Above the folders it says what such a count cannot see: the folders the agent could not read (it runs as its user), the space in no folder counted (those folders, or files deleted while a program still holds them open), and, for /, what docker and the system journal say they keep. A machine's Overview leads there from its Disk card.

Packages is every package dpkg has installed there, read the same way: its version, its size, whether it was installed by hand or came along as another package's need, and — from apt-get -s upgrade --with-new-pkgs, a dry run that needs no root — the version an upgrade would bring, marked when it comes from a security archive. Held and half-installed packages say so. The dry run reads the lists the last apt-get update left, so "to update" is as fresh as those; the Configure tab installs them.

An upgrade can restart Docker, and Docker does not bring back every container it stopped. Before it starts, serviceman notes the containers that run; once it is over, it waits for Docker to answer and starts again each one that is not running. What cannot start is named at the end of the upgrade's lines, with Docker's reason, and on the Health page.

#Its updates

A machine's Configure tab says what apt has waiting, and Install them runs apt-get update, then apt-get upgrade --with-new-pkgs (an update that brings a new package with it, a new kernel's, is installed too; nothing is removed), answering its questions as a person would and keeping every config file you changed. Every line apt prints is shown while it runs; Cancel stops it. A root agent runs apt-get; one that runs as a user runs sudo -n apt-get, so sudo on that machine has to let it without a password.

What is waiting is counted by apt, with the same upgrade as a dry run, so a machine just upgraded says nothing waits; it is counted again whenever what is installed, or what apt knows of, changes. Ubuntu's own count, on its login banner, is larger: it counts a full upgrade, with what upgrade keeps back. What apt keeps back even so, mostly phased updates Ubuntu hands out to a few machines at a time, is shown apart as held back: it is not waiting on you, and Install does not count it.

Install updates on N, at the top of Remotes, does the same on every machine the list shows that has something waiting: the filter and the chips narrow it, and each machine can be unticked. They all start at once, each its own apt, with a row each for how it goes and its last line; a row opens the machine's Configure tab with every line. The machine serviceman itself runs on waits until the others end, then runs alone: an upgrade of Docker there restarts serviceman in the middle of it. serviceman finds that machine by its own container in the machine's docker ps. Cancel all stops what runs and what waits. The runs are serviceman's, not the page's: a closed page stops nothing, and the list shows them again when opened.

After an upgrade, every container that ran before it runs again: the ones Docker does not bring back, serviceman starts. A machine that wants a restart says so; nothing restarts it.

The calls, for a script: POST /api/v1/apt-upgrade with {"remotes": ["vps1", "vps2"]} starts them and answers which started, which waits (held) and which were left out and why; GET /api/v1/apt-upgrade is a row per machine; POST /api/v1/apt-cancel stops them. One machine's are the Packages module's: POST /api/v1/remotes/<name>/packages/upgrade starts it and answers the stream of its lines, {stream, url}, read at url as it goes; GET at the same address is where it stands, and POST …/packages/cancel stops it.

#Its ports and its firewall

The Firewall tab of a remote is what the machine listens on and what its firewall, ufw, lets through. (It was two tabs, Ports and Firewall; an old /ports address opens it.)

The ports are everything the machine is listening on — tcp and udp, v4 and v6 — with what is holding each socket, one row per port and holder, read with ss when the tab opens and when Read again is pressed. Each says who its address lets reach it: the internet (a public address, or every address of a machine that has a public one), a network (a private range, link-local, or the tailnet's 100.64.0.0/10), or this machine only (loopback). Beside it, what the firewall does to it: let in by a rule, kept out by a rule or by the default, or, while the firewall is off, what it will do once on. ufw goes by the first rule that matches, so that is the rule named; a rule for one source only is said beside it ("kept out by the default, but from 10.0.0.0/8"). Allow on a row adds a rule for that port; Close takes away the rule that let it in, with Undo. The tiles count what actually gets through: a port the firewall keeps out is counted as kept out, however open its address. A firewall in front of the machine (a cloud's security group) is not seen from here.

ss names the holder of a socket only to whoever may read that socket, and the agent in a person's session may read its own and no others — so the port list is asked of the machine's root half where it has one, and every daemon on it is named. A machine with no root half, or one whose root half is older than this, answers as the session agent: the same ports, with the Held by column filled in for its own and empty for the rest.

The rules are ufw's own, on or off: its defaults, a row to add one, and × to delete one, with Undo that puts it back at its old place. A rule that lets ssh in is asked for before the firewall goes on without one; serviceman itself is never shut out, since its agent dials out. ufw runs as root: in the machine's root half where it has one, else as sudo -n ufw, which needs a sudoers line naming ufw. A machine without ufw says so; a root half older than the firewall says it is updating. The module is modules/firewall, and its README has the API.

#Its encrypted volumes

An encrypted volume is one file on one machine's disk, LUKS with ext4 inside, opened at a folder of that machine: a stolen disk or snapshot shows random bytes and a size. The Storage page lists every machine's volumes under its folders: the folder, open or closed, how full, and what the file takes on the disk. Close and Grow are in a volume's row; a close that something still holds says what holds it, a process or a container, and closes nothing; a systemd service's sandbox, which only sees the mount, holds nothing. New volume… makes one with a passphrase you type, kept nowhere, and Open… in its row opens it again: you type it after every reboot, and a lost one opens it never. A typed passphrase is hashed with argon2id at the cost cryptsetup measures on the machine. Visual Agents makes and opens its own through the API, with keys it holds. The work is the machine's root half's, and a key travels only over TLS, a socket file, the same machine, a page loaded from this machine's localhost or the tailnet. The module is modules/volumes, and its README has the API.

#When something is wrong

Every minute serviceman looks at everything it runs and knows, and the Health page, first in the rail, shows what it found: one row per thing (a machine, a service, Logline and each machine's lines, a forward), and one check per thing it does, green when it works, orange when it works but wants a look, red when it does not, grey when there is nothing to say yet. What is wrong comes first, one card each: where it is, since when, why, and what mends it; a red bar under the page's header says so on every page and opens it. Its × puts it away once the problems are seen, in this browser; a problem not seen yet brings it back, and the Health row of the rail stays red meanwhile. A problem shows once it is seen twice in a row, so a blip of a second is not one, and leaves on its own once it is mended. Each is written to the log too, problem_begin and problem_end (The log).

It looks for How
A machine that was here and went offline Its link.
A copy of a service that does not answer A request to it, the way a visitor's goes.
A container Docker was meant to keep running, down Docker cannot start it, it keeps failing, or on-failure gave up; one stopped by hand is not, whatever its exit code.
A running container whose mounted files are gone Each bind mount looked for on the machine: it runs on what it holds open, and will not start again after a restart.
Lines Logline does not take What Logline answered the machine last, how long nothing went while lines wait, and how full the machine's store is.
Logline's viewer not answering A request to it, the way Open Logline goes.

Health shows the rest beside them, said but not counted as problems, one table per part with a column per check; a click on a row opens every check's detail under it. Logline's store counts as working while the machines' lines are taken: its address is theirs to reach, and serviceman may not be able to look it up.

Check Orange or red when
Agent It runs an older agent than serviceman serves, or will not update (it says why).
Disk Under 10% of the disk is free; red under 3%.
Memory, CPU Under 5% of the memory is free; the CPU is 90% busy or more.
Updates Security updates wait, or the machine wants a restart after an upgrade.
Firewall ufw is installed and off. Asked every five minutes, one ufw status; grey where ufw is not there.
Doors The machine did not take its door table.
Forwards A forward cannot listen, or one of its two machines is away.

#When the machine is away

What you see What it means
remote vps1: offline, the link held 4h 2m The link dropped. The agent dials in again.
[remote_service_lost] service=kept remote=vps1 Its containers keep running over there.
502 remote vps1 is offline — its agent is not dialled in A visitor asked for a service on a dead remote.
remote vps1: an agent dialled in with the wrong token Someone knocked with the wrong secret.

A service on that machine reads lost while the link is down, not stopped: nobody stopped it, and this host simply cannot see it. The address it last answered on is kept, and the page says why.

The agent dials again after 1s, then 2s, doubling to 30s, for as long as it takes. When it comes back, a container still running over there is adopted, not started twice, a container that has gone becomes stopped, and a service with "start": "always" is started then.

#Dialling in over a socket file

An agent does not need a port at all:

node serviceman-agent.js --url unix:///run/serviceman-control.sock --token 0c0f…a91b

That is the same door the control page answers on (control.socket). Forward it and the machine can be anywhere:

ssh -R /run/serviceman-control.sock:/run/serviceman-control.sock vps1

Now the agent on that box dials a file, serviceman listens on nothing, and no port is open at either end.

#Reaching this host

The service port is bound to 127.0.0.1 until the config widens it, so an agent on another machine has nothing to dial yet. Give it an address:

"listen": {"host": "0.0.0.0", "port": 8080}

The control page does not open with it — it still answers only the machine serviceman runs on. The remote door is the one thing on that port a stranger may knock at, and the token is what gets them in.

#A machine that takes the traffic

Beside the agent is http.sock, and whatever connects to it is answered by the agent itself. A machine that owns a public address needs nothing on it but the agent: no serviceman, no port open to one, and no tunnel of your own.

The agent routes; serviceman only writes the table. For each name its door answers, the agent asks the wall in front of it, and only when the wall was reached and said yes carries the request to the service — straight to it on this machine, or to the agent of the machine it runs on, over the tailnet. serviceman writes each machine the table it routes by — its names, where each service they need runs, how to reach the other machines' agents — and the machine keeps it on its own disk (doors/table.json, beside the agent). serviceman is in none of the traffic: with it down, the doors go on answering from the table they hold, and a machine that restarts meanwhile serves what it served before.

What the table cannot route still goes to serviceman over the link, as every request did before the doors routed themselves: a name the table does not have, a service serviceman answers itself. Those stop when serviceman does.

A service on this machine is found the way it is now: a container by asking docker for the port it has — and starting it first, if it is stopped, which is how a sleeping service wakes with serviceman away — a program by its port, an address serviceman does not start by that address. A container that does not exist yet is serviceman's to make. Requests through the door count as the service being in use: serviceman does not stop as idle what a door is keeping busy.

A service on another machine is asked of that machine's agent: each agent listens for its peers on its tailnet addresses, port 7303 (--peer-port, SERVICEMAN_PEER_PORT; 0 turns it off), and answers only a caller holding the token serviceman gave it, and only for the services that run on it. The Doors page says, for each machine, whether it routes by itself and holds the latest table.

There is no door until one is asked for. --http-socket-mode 0660 (or SERVICEMAN_HTTP_SOCKET_MODE in the agent's env) is the whole of the asking: without it the agent opens nothing, and a machine carries requests in only because somebody said it should.

The mode is also the whole of who may knock — 0660 and a group for that machine's web server, 0600 for nobody but the user the agent runs as. The door stands for the life of the agent, link or no link.

upstream serviceman {
    server unix:/home/you/serviceman-agent/http.sock;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name devservice.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://serviceman;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        # the door routes by this name and nothing else
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
        # an event stream goes out as it comes, an upload as large as the service takes
        proxy_buffering off;
        client_max_body_size 0;
    }
}

A door answers the names it was given, and none at all by default. A rule is a name and the service that takes it, written on the machine's own entry. A service's page lists its public addresses and adds, switches and removes them; the Doors page has every machine's:

{"name": "laptop", "token": "0c0f…a91b", "inbound": {"echo.example.com": "echo", "*.example.com": "site"}}

The name is not the service's own address: echo goes on publishing whatever it publishes, and this is a name it also answers to, on that machine's front. Nothing has to be renamed to be served from another machine.

A rule can be set aside without being taken away — the name keeps its place and stops answering, which is what an afternoon of quiet wants rather than retyping it later:

"inbound": {"echo.example.com": {"service": "echo", "off": true}}

#A wall in front of a name

auth names a service to ask before anything behind it is touched — authwall, or anything that answers the same door:

"inbound": {
    "sam.example.com": {"service": "notes", "auth": "authwall"},
    "*.example.com":   {"service": "site",  "auth": "authwall"}
}

Nothing is proxied through the wall. The door asks it GET /auth/sidecar with the name that was asked for, the whole address, the visitor's cookie and their address, and reads the answer:

The wall says The door does
200 Answers with the service, carrying the wall's X-Auth-User to it.
401 or 403 Sends the visitor to /auth/sign-in?return=… on the name they asked for.
nothing, or else Answers 502 and touches nothing behind it: a wall that cannot be asked is a closed door.

/auth/… on a walled name is the wall's own: its sign-in page, its callbacks. That is what lets the sign-in happen on the visitor's own address rather than somewhere else.

One wall stands in front of as many names as point at it. It never learns where any of them lead, so nothing about it changes when a rule does. The wall may run on any machine: the door reaches it the way it reaches any service. serviceman writes nothing into its environment: the wall's own name (AUTHWALL_PUBLIC_URL), the cookie domain shared by the names it guards (AUTHWALL_COOKIE_DOMAIN), and who may sign in (AUTHWALL_ALLOWED_EMAILS) are yours, and are the whole of what it needs.

The service behind a wall is untouched — it keeps its own address, and answers there as it always did. Whatever a visitor claims about themselves in X-Auth-User is dropped: what the service reads is the wall's word.

#A port at home, on a public name

A port of a computer with no public address (the laptop, behind the home router) is served on a name of the machine that has one. It is an external service on the laptop and a rule on the machine, nothing more:

"remotes": [
    {"name": "vps1", "token": "0c0f…a91b", "inbound": {"phone.example.com": "phone-door"}},
    {"name": "laptop", "token": "5e1d…07c2"}
],
"services": [
    {"name": "phone-door", "type": "external", "remote": "laptop", "publish": {"host": "phone-door.localhost"}, "upstream": "127.0.0.1:8771"}
]

The request comes in at vps1's front, its door hands it to the laptop's agent over the tailnet, and that agent carries it to 127.0.0.1:8771. Nothing at home opens to the internet, and the port may stay bound to the loopback. The body is streamed both ways, so an upload and an event stream that stays open for hours pass as they are; whatever the front sets (an upload limit, a read timeout, buffering) still holds, and so does a CDN's (Cloudflare drops a stream quiet for 100 seconds). Both are in the config, so they outlive a restart of either side.

What a door carries is marked. Every request it carries gets X-Serviceman-Relay: 1, set over whatever the visitor sent, so a service that lets more in at home (a pairing, a first sign-in) can refuse it to whoever came through a door. Who they are is in X-Forwarded-For, as the front wrote it.

When the laptop is away (asleep, off, off the tailnet), the door waits 10 seconds for a connection and answers 502. A front or a CDN may answer for it with a 5xx of its own, so a client reads any 502, 503, 504 or 52x as "not reachable now".

#A port or a socket from one machine to another

A forward makes a port of one machine show up on another, the way ssh -L does, with no ssh: the machines' links to serviceman carry it. from is where the service is, to where it shows up. A Loki on vps1's loopback, as a socket file on the laptop:

"forwards": [
    {"label": "Loki on vps1", "from": {"remote": "vps1", "port": 3100}, "to": {"remote": "laptop", "socket": "~/repos/loki.sock"}}
]

The laptop's agent listens on ~/repos/loki.sock. Each connection opens a stream over its link to serviceman, serviceman opens one over vps1's link to 127.0.0.1:3100, and joins the two. A port works as well as a socket at either end, and a service at home brought to a server is the same thing written the other way round.

  • The socket stays. The agent keeps listening while its link is down: a connection then is closed at once, and the first one after the redial goes through. A dead ssh holds a socket for as long as its keep-alives take to notice; a forward has none to wait for.
  • Nobody else's. A socket file is 0600, for the agent's user alone; a port is bound to 127.0.0.1. A machine may open only the forwards whose to is itself: one that names another machine's forward is refused, and nothing is dialled for it.
  • A socket someone else answers on is theirs. An ssh -L already on that path keeps it; the page says the forward cannot listen, and it is tried again every minute. A file left by a process that is gone is taken over.
  • What it says. The Doors page lists every forward: where it listens, whether a connection would go through now and if not why (vps2 is offline, the agent on laptop is older than forwards — update it), the connections open and in all, the bytes each way, and the last failure.

Both ends run the agent, so a host that runs none (a box you only ssh into) still needs ssh. A forward carries bytes and nothing else: what is spoken over it is between the two programs.

#A forward onto serviceman itself

to may be serviceman itself instead of a machine: "here": true in place of remote. serviceman then listens in place of an agent, and the machine with the service is the only one that needs one. vps1's Loki, as a socket file beside serviceman:

"forwards": [
    {"label": "Loki on vps1", "from": {"remote": "vps1", "port": 3100}, "to": {"here": true, "socket": "sockets/loki.sock"}}
]
  • Where the socket lands. In serviceman's state dir (SERVICEMAN_STATE_DIR), written from it: sockets/loki.sock is data/sockets/loki.sock. A path from / or ~/, or one that goes up with .., is refused. Its folder is made when it is missing. bin/run already mounts the host's ./data at /app/data, the state dir in the image, so the socket is on the host's disk at ./data/sockets/loki.sock with no extra docker mount.
  • Whose it is. The socket is 0600. A serviceman that runs as root, as it does in a rootful docker, gives it, and any folder it made for it, to whoever owns the state dir: on the host, the person who owns ./data opens it, and nobody else. Any other serviceman keeps it for its own user.
  • A port ("port": 3100) listens on serviceman's own 127.0.0.1. Under bin/run that is the container's loopback, which the host does not reach; a socket is the way out of it.
  • The rest is a forward like any other. A connection while vps1 is away is closed at once and the reason is kept; a file left by a serviceman that crashed is taken over, a file that is not a socket is never deleted, and a socket that cannot listen is tried again every minute and shown on the page. A forward set aside or taken out of the config closes, and its file goes.

#Through a reverse proxy

The agent asks for an HTTP upgrade on /api/v1/remote, the same shape as a websocket. nginx and caddy carry it with their usual websocket block; give it a long read timeout, because the link is quiet between requests.

location /api/v1/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_read_timeout 1h;
}

A CDN in front will not hold a link open for hours. Point the agent at the origin.

#What the token buys

Whoever has the token can dial in as that remote. Then this host will run containers on that machine, read their logs, make folders for their volumes, and reach any port on its loopback through the tunnel. Treat it like an ssh key: one token per machine, 32 random bytes, kept in a file only root can read.

The other direction is narrow, but not empty. The agent does what it is asked and nothing else: docker commands, a folder for a bind mount, and streams — to a port on its own loopback, or to its docker socket, which is how a shell in one of its containers is opened from here. A forward's listener is the one way a connection on the machine reaches the host, and only under a forward's label. That socket is docker itself, so a remote trusts this host as much as this host trusts whoever reaches its control page. Its firewall too: ufw's rules are written from the control page, as root. The agent runs no shell of its own for the host, and it never dials anywhere except the --url you gave it.

#Not built yet

  • A compose stack cannot be run by an agent.
  • Nothing is placed automatically: you name the remote, or the service does not run.
